newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish central bank sees no zloty rise in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Polish central bank sees no zloty rise in 1997.

text.p: The Polish zloty has little upside potential next year and pressure for devaluation may emerge if the current account balance of payments gap widens more than expected, the central bank's deputy president, Witold Kozinski, said on Monday.
"One should not expect a real effective zloty appreciation next year we are saying it openly...," he told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

The National Bank of Poland assumed in its 1997 monetary policy draft that the zloty's parity rate -- the centre of the domestic market's 14 percent trading band -- would be gradually devalued against a basket of currencies by nine percent.

But Kozinski said market pressure to push the zloty below the trading band's centre might emerge if foreign reserves, expected to stabilise next year, began to fall. The zloty now trades at about two percent above the parity rate.
"There will likely be a situation that a (relative) scarcity of currencies will translate into pressure on zloty devaluation against the basket of currencies," he said.
The zloty is now devalued by one percent per month, 12.7 percent per year, against a basket of western currencies.

In its monetary policy draft the NBP did not rule out allowing the market to push the zloty below the parity rate but Kozinski said it would keep the market guessing over how and when the bank would intervene to support the Polish unit.

"We have a nominal devaluation of nine percent against the central parity rate and the rest is now unknown. If devaluation pressure emerges we will ask ourselves...if such a devaluation would already have an inflationary effect or not and...whether to stabilise the market," he said.
Kozinski said occasional intervention to halt speculative zloty rallies and adjustments of the crawling devaluation rate could not be ruled out.
The central bank predicts a trade deficit of about $9.5 billion but assumes that the shortfall will be roughly balanced by cross-border inflows and capital flows, mainly in direct foreign investment.
Kozinski said however portfolio investment in fixed income instruments, mainly T-bills would be contained by the bearish zloty outlook.
"I believe we will not have a problem of short-term capital inflows in 1997," he said.
"A careful student of our policy has to conclude that 1997 won't be a year of real zloty appreciation and that one should invest in other instruments than T-bills," Kozinski said.
Asked about the exchange rate mechanism Kozinski said the crawling devaluation has served the Polish economy well and the central bank saw no need for changes next year.

"There have been suggestions to peg the zloty to some currency...but the zloty still has to be devalued against the basket as inflation is still too high and such an exchange rate shock...would be too big," he said.
